d.title: What speech takes away, and why the latency budget is the obvious half
d.caption: Modelling a voice agent as a chat agent with audio bolted to each end fails for a reason more interesting than latency: **the interface affordances your text product relies on stop existing.** No delete key, so a mistyped name is never fixed before it is sent. No scrollback, so a caller holds the conversation in working memory instead of re-reading it. Every mitigation that depends on the user seeing and revising is gone.

d.title: Five perception bands, and the two numbers worth memorising
d.caption: Latency does not degrade experience linearly — **crossing a threshold changes what the user believes is happening.** The two to memorise are **800 ms**, under which a turn feels responsive, and **1,200 ms**, over which it reads as thinking. The cascaded pipeline in 13.3 lands at **1,650 ms — in the band where users repeat themselves**, which is the worst possible place to be, because the repeat arrives mid-response and triggers an interruption on a turn that was merely slow.

d.title: Identical medians, 17.1% against 96.1% bad calls
d.caption: Time to first audio is **heavy-tailed** — a sum of stages, several with long right tails — so the median says almost nothing on its own. Two agents with an **identical 700 ms median** give 70.3% responsive turns against 57.1%, and the conjunction over a twelve-turn call amplifies it: **17.1% of calls go badly against 96.1%**. A call is not one draw from the distribution; it is twelve, and the width parameter is what decides the product.

d.title: Three things to check before approving a faster model
d.caption: The scenario: a text eval scoring 0.91 task success and a median time to first audio of 1,400 ms, and a proposal to buy a faster model. **Check the p95 first** — above 1,500 ms you have a variance problem and a faster median will not fix it. Check whether the eval was run on audio, because 13.12 measures a text harness reporting 100% where the real figure is 38%. And check the endpointer: **13.3 shows halving the model's TTFT buys 10.6% while endpointing is 42.4% of the budget.** A faster model is on the list, fourth.

d.title: Speech-native removes the ASR latency and keeps the ASR bill
d.caption: This is the detail that breaks most speech-native cost models. **You still need a transcript** — for quality review, dispute resolution, the eval set, any text-based guardrail, and in a regulated industry because you are required to have one. So you run recognition over the call anyway. The good news: **it is off the critical path**, so it can run after the call, in batch, at a cheaper tier, adding zero latency. The bad news: **it costs the same money it did in the cascade.**

d.title: Seven situations, and the default for anyone who has not measured
d.caption: Two rows are about **boundaries rather than quality**: regulated work and tool-heavy agents need text between thought and speech, and you cannot bolt that on afterwards. The last row is the honest default: **cascade, because it is the one you can instrument** — and 13.3 shows most of the 730 ms gap is recoverable for free, so the choice is rarely as forced as it looks.

d.title: Halving each stage, and where the roadmap should go
d.caption: A budget tells you where the time is; **a sensitivity analysis tells you what an improvement is worth**, which is the question a roadmap needs. Halving a stage is a rough unit of serious engineering effort. The answer is unambiguous: **endpointing is 42.4% of the budget and halving it buys 21.2%**, against 10.6% for halving the model's time to first token. Three of the seven stages are worth under 4% each, which is where attention usually goes.

d.title: 1,650 against 920, and 200 ms of it is one threshold
d.caption: The speech-native pipeline is **the only one of the two that lands inside 13.1's responsive band**. The cascade at 1,650 ms sits where users repeat themselves. That is not a marginal difference in a metric — it is a different product. And note where the gap comes from: of the 730 ms, **200 ms is the endpoint threshold alone**, which is a configuration choice rather than an architectural one.

d.title: A sensitivity ranking is not a plan
d.caption: A sensitivity analysis ranks changes **individually**, and a target needs combinations — whose costs do not add the way milliseconds do. **Two optimisations might save 300 ms between them, cost ten engineering weeks and raise the per-call price; a third might save 200 ms for a configuration change.** So the ranking is the input to a plan rather than the plan: order by milliseconds per unit of effort and risk, not by milliseconds.

d.title: Five blocks of arithmetic, and no audio library anywhere
d.caption: Worth noticing what kind of program this is: **no audio library, no model call, no network — arithmetic over a table of constants.** And it is still the most useful artefact in the module, because **the constants are the design and the arithmetic is the argument.** A voice pipeline is a latency allocation problem before it is an engineering one, and this is the form in which that problem can be argued about.

d.title: A table that says why each stage exists is a table you can argue with
d.caption: **A table of stage names and durations invites someone to ask for all of them to be smaller.** A table that also says *why* each one exists turns every row into a trade with a named cost. Then "reduce the playout buffer to 30 ms" is visibly **a decision to accept more gaps mid-word on bad connections**, rather than a free 30 ms — and the conversation moves from optimisation to policy, which is where it belongs.

d.title: The endpointing frontier, as a probability
d.caption: Model intra-utterance pauses as lognormal with a 220 ms median, and for any threshold **the fraction of pauses longer than it is exactly the fraction of turns the agent talks over.** That turns a tuning knob into a frontier you can read: **300 ms cuts off 34 turns in 100; 700 ms cuts off 6.1; 1,200 ms cuts off 1.2** — and every step down that column is paid for in latency on *every* turn, not just the interrupted ones.

d.title: A silence timer listens to the one signal that is least informative
d.caption: The standard rule — no speech for N ms, so the turn is over — **is wrong in a way no amount of tuning fixes**, because people pause inside sentences for reasons that have nothing to do with being finished. Meanwhile **a genuine end of turn is often marked by no silence at all**: a falling pitch contour, a completed syntactic structure, a question's rising tone. Humans use those, which is why their turn-taking gap is 200 ms rather than 700 — and a silence timer discards every one of them.

d.title: The frontier, with the latency cost beside it
d.caption: The table is usually read as a tuning guide and it is really a **frontier**: each threshold buys an interruption rate at the price of adding the same number of milliseconds to **every** turn. 300 ms cuts off 34 turns in 100; 1,500 ms cuts off 0.5 and adds 1.5 seconds to all of them. There is no setting on this curve that is good — which is §04's point, because a semantic endpointer is not a point on it.

d.title: The stuttering demo, and why headphones hide it
d.caption: Before any of the rest works, **the agent must not hear itself.** If the microphone picks up the speaker output — which it does on a laptop, a phone handset, a speakerphone and a car — the voice activity detector sees speech for the entire time the agent is talking, and **barge-in fires immediately and continuously**. The agent speaks two or three words, cuts out, starts again, cuts out, with nobody talking to it. **On headphones everything works perfectly**, which is why this ships.

d.title: "As I already mentioned" is a state bug, not a hallucination
d.caption: **The model is reading its own transcript correctly** — the transcript is wrong. When a user interrupts, the generated text that was never spoken stays in the history, so the model believes it said things the user never heard. That is what makes it a **state-management bug rather than a model-quality bug**, and why no amount of prompting fixes it: truncate the assistant turn to what was actually played out. 13.15 prices the omission at **17.5% phantom context over a ten-turn call.**

d.title: Every stage has something useful to say before it is done
d.caption: The naive pipeline treats each stage as a function and every stage waits for its predecessor. The streamed pipeline treats each as a **generator**. The unit that matters in the middle is the **clause**: you do not synthesise token by token, because prosody — pitch, stress, the shape of a phrase — depends on where the phrase ends, so **a clause of roughly twelve tokens is the smallest unit that sounds natural.** And playout emits nothing, but it can be **flushed**, which is what makes barge-in possible at all.

d.title: Streaming saves 420 ms of the response and zero of the first audio
d.caption: The full response goes from 2,410 ms serial to 1,990 ms streamed — **420 ms, widening with the length of the answer**, because every additional clause is additive in a serial pipeline and hidden in a streamed one. And **time to first audio is 1,650 ms in both. Not approximately — identically, to the millisecond.** The path to the first sound is a chain: endpointing, finalisation, network, prefill, one clause, synthesis, playout. Overlapping stages cannot shorten a chain; **only removing a link can**, which is §03.

d.title: Speculative prefill removes a link instead of overlapping one
d.caption: During the endpointing window — **700 ms of deliberate waiting** — the pipeline is doing nothing at all, and it already has a partial transcript that is probably close to final. So prefill on it. The saving depends entirely on **how much of the speculative prefill survives**: if the partial's prefix is byte-identical to the final prompt's prefix, everything up to the divergence point is reusable. Measured: **175 ms if half is reusable, 290 ms if nearly all of it is.**
